Happy Union
hap'-i ū'-nyun
n. (the Happy Union, 1691–1695, the short-lived agreement of London Presbyterians and Congregationalists)
Middle English hap, chance, fortune, whence happy; Latin unio, oneness.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Happy Union was the agreement of 1691 by which the Presbyterian and Congregational ministers in and about London formed a single body under Heads of Agreement, pooling their funds, their lecture, and their examination of candidates. The old quarrel of the 1640s over church government had been worn down by thirty years of shared suffering under the Clarendon Code, and with toleration granted in 1689 both sides thought the breach could be closed. It lasted four years. The trouble came not over polity but over doctrine: Richard Davis of Rothwell was accused of antinomian preaching, and in the controversy that followed the republication of Tobias Crisp's sermons divided the union into parties, the Presbyterians suspecting antinomianism and the Congregationalists suspecting neonomianism. By 1695 the common fund was split and the union was over, though the Heads of Agreement remained in print as a standing proposal. “Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another” (Rom 14:19) — it proved easier to subscribe than to practise.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines union as the junction of two or more things, concord; and agreement as harmony of opinion or sentiment.

expand to see more

U'NION, n. The act of joining two or more things into one; concord; agreement.

AGREE'MENT, n. Harmony of opinion, action or character; a compact or bargain.

FUND, n. A stock or capital; money set apart for a specific purpose.

Key Scripture

Rom 14:19 — "Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another."

Eph 4:3 — "Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace."

1Co 1:10 — "Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment."

Jam 3:18 — "And the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace of them that make peace."

Modern Corruption

The 1691 London union of Presbyterians and Congregationalists, broken in four years.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Happy Union is instructive precisely because it failed over the thing nobody expected. Both sides had braced for a fight about elders and synods, the issue that had divided them for fifty years; what broke them was the gospel itself — how free the offer is, and what place the law has in a believer's standing.

The principle to recover is that peace is something followed after, with an aim: “things wherewith one may edify another” (Rom 14:19). A union whose only shared ground is a shared grievance will not survive the first doctrinal question, and the fruit of righteousness “is sown in peace of them that make peace” (Jam 3:18) — sown, that is, by patient work and not by a signature.

Usage

"“follow after the things which make for peace” (Rom 14:19) — the Heads of Agreement, 1691."

"“that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10) — what four years could not secure."

"“the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace” (Jam 3:18) — and it takes longer than a signature."
